title: Beyond Maximum Likelihood: Variational Inequality Estimation for Generalized Linear Models
claim: Under saturating or clipped links, the likelihood-loss gradient becomes spiky and discontinuous, while the operator-based vector field stays monotone and well-behaved.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, shared legend on top, same x-axis
description: Three side-by-side line plots share the x-axis β from -6 to 6 and a top legend with three clipped-exponential settings (c=0, C=1 in solid blue; c=0.5, C=3 in orange dash-dot; c=1, C=5 in green dashed). The left panel shows the MLE loss L(β). The blue curve is a smooth convex bowl, while the orange and green curves go flat on both sides of the minimum at β=0 and plateau at different heights. The middle panel shows the loss derivative ∇L(β). The blue curve is smooth, while the orange and green curves have sharp vertical spikes and drop to zero. The right panel shows the VI vector field V(β). All three curves are monotone and increase smoothly, then saturate at different levels. The eye goes first to the colored dashed curves and the jagged middle panel.

abstract: Generalized linear models (GLMs) are fundamental tools for statistical modeling, with maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) serving as the classical approach for parameter inference. While MLE performs well for canonical GLMs, it can become computationally challenging in more general settings with non-canonical, non-smooth, or saturating link functions, where the resulting optimization landscape may be ill-conditioned, non-convex, or non-differentiable. In this paper, we study an alternative estimation framework based on variational inequalities (VIs), which formulates GLM estimation through an operator-based equilibrium condition rather than likelihood minimization. We analyze the VI estimator from a statistical perspective and establish finite-sample error bounds and asymptotic normality, together with convergence guarantees for fixed-point and stochastic approximation algorithms. The framework accommodates a broad class of link functions, including non-canonical, non-smooth, and non-monotone cases satisfying a strong Minty-type condition, and extends naturally to generalized additive models (GAMs) via basis expansion. Numerical experiments demonstrate that under a fixed iteration budget, the VI approach achieves competitive estimation accuracy and faster, more stable convergence than MLE, particularly in GLMs and GAMs with non-canonical or non-smooth link functions.
